Phylogenetically varying slopes

Source: R/kernels_slope.R
k_slope.Rd

k_slope(x) * k multiplies a kernel k by x_i x_j, the kernel of a regression slope on x whose deviations from the mean slope evolve along the tree under k:

Usage

k_slope(x, center = TRUE, latent = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Name of a column of the data passed to phylo_gp(), or a numeric vector named by tip label.

center

Centre x at its mean over the fitted species?

latent

Sample the slope deviations at the nodes (linear time) rather than use the dense marginal kernel.

Value

An object to be multiplied by one kernel component.

Details

$$y_i = \beta_0 + (\beta_1 + v_i) x_i + \dots, \quad v \sim GP(0, k).$$

  • k_slope(x) * k_bm() (or another branch-wise kernel): the slope evolves along the tree. The covariance is sigma^2 (x x') o K, valid whenever K is (Schur product theorem).

  • k_slope(x) * k_white(): independent species-specific slope deviations, i.e. residual variance that grows with x^2. This is the natural control for a varying-slope model: a varying slope also makes the variance of y grow with distance from the centre of x, and comparing the two kernels separates evolving slopes from heteroscedasticity.

The mean slope is the regression coefficient of x in the model formula, so x should normally appear there as well. Because the kernel depends on where x is centred, x is centred at its mean by default; report the centring with the results.

With latent = TRUE (default) the slope deviations at the nodes of the tree are sampled as latent variables and the remaining Gaussian components are integrated out by pruning, so the cost per gradient stays linear in the number of species; this needs method = "sample". With latent = FALSE the dense marginal kernel is used (O(N^3)), which also allows maximum likelihood.

References

Lande R. 1979. Quantitative genetic analysis of multivariate evolution, applied to brain:body size allometry. Evolution. 33:402–416.

Pagel M.D., Harvey P.H. 1989. Taxonomic differences in the scaling of brain on body weight among mammals. Science. 244:1589–1593.

Hadfield J.D., Nakagawa S. 2010. General quantitative genetic methods for comparative biology: Phylogenies, taxonomies and multi-trait models for continuous and categorical characters. Journal of Evolutionary Biology. 23:494–508.

Matsuba M., Fukasawa K., Aoki S., Akasaka M., Ishihama F. 2024. Scalable phylogenetic Gaussian process models improve the detectability of environmental signals on local extinctions for many Red List species. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. 15:756–768.

Examples

k_bm() + k_slope("body") * k_bm() + k_white()      # varying slopes
#> phylogp kernel: bm() + slope(body) * bm() + white() 
#>   bm1        bm()                         parameters: sigma
#>   slopebm1   slope(body) * bm()           parameters: sigma, (latent values)
#>   white1     white()                      parameters: sigma
k_bm() + k_slope("body") * k_white() + k_white()   # heteroscedastic control
#> phylogp kernel: bm() + slope(body) * white() + white() 
#>   bm1        bm()                         parameters: sigma
#>   slopewhite1 slope(body) * white()        parameters: sigma
#>   white1     white()                      parameters: sigma
